AI Companies Have a Distribution Problem Disguised as a Model Problem.

By lowob · 15 June 2026 · Updated 10 November 2026 · 4-minute read · Distribution / AI

A company can build an impressive AI product, show a great demo, and still struggle to find paying customers. The problem may not be that the model needs another improvement. It may be that the company hasn't worked out who needs the product, why they should trust it, or how they'll discover it.

Model quality matters. But better model performance doesn't automatically create a distribution system. Customers are buying a way to complete a job, not a benchmark score.

A better model isn't a go-to-market plan

Picture a small AI company that can summarize and search internal contracts. Its team spends weeks improving response quality. Meanwhile, the potential buyers are asking different questions: Can we connect it to the documents we already use? Who can see sensitive information? How would we check an incorrect answer? Who owns the rollout?

The demonstration proves a capability. It doesn't yet make the product easy to adopt. This is a hypothetical example, but it captures the gap between building something useful and persuading an organization to depend on it.

A company can still need better technology. The point is to distinguish product problems from distribution and adoption problems before deciding what to build next.

Name the buyer and the job they need done

“Businesses that want to use AI” is too broad to guide marketing. “Legal operations teams that spend hours finding clauses across supplier contracts” is more specific. It points to a job, a person responsible for it, a current alternative and a meaningful outcome.

Start with three questions: Who has the problem often enough to pay? What do they do today instead? What would convince them to change? Interview buyers rather than answering from the product team's imagination.

Not every AI product needs to own an entire workflow. Some successful products are focused components inside systems customers already use. In either case, the integration and the end result matter more to adoption than the isolated model demo.

Show what the product does, and where it can fail

Trust grows when people can inspect the work. A short demonstration with a real workflow, realistic inputs and clearly identified limitations is more persuasive than a claim that the tool is “revolutionary.” In higher-stakes uses, explain what happens when the system is uncertain and how people can review its output.

For the contract product, useful proof might include sample tasks, permission controls, a documented evaluation process and feedback from a pilot customer, with the customer's permission. Avoid claiming a universal accuracy rate based on a small internal test.

The team should record objections from sales calls and use them to improve the product, the explanation and the onboarding process.

Build channels that reach the people doing the work

Generic AI announcements compete with thousands of similar launches. An industry practitioner demonstrating a workflow, an integration into software buyers already use, or a useful comparison published where teams research solutions may do more to reach a qualified buyer.

Prioritize a few channels you can test: direct conversations with target accounts, credible practitioner partnerships, integrations and instructional content. Add paid acquisition where the economics make sense and the claims are supportable. Keep the resulting contacts and learning in systems the company controls.

Choose a distribution approach that remains useful even if the underlying models improve or suppliers change.

Measure adoption, not demo applause

Track the path from a relevant conversation to a trial, a completed job, repeat use and, when applicable, paid retention. If the product's value is saving time, measure the quality of the result alongside the time saved. A faster answer that creates rework is not a win.

When prospects consistently fail at setup, improve onboarding. When nobody can explain the return, improve proof. When the right people never see the product, improve distribution. Those are different problems, and they deserve different responses.

lowob takeaways

  • Separate capability from adoption. A better model alone won't fix a missing buyer or channel.
  • Sell a specific job. State who needs the product, what they do today and what improves.
  • Make proof easy to inspect. Real workflow examples and honest limitations build more trust than broad claims.
  • Measure repeat use. Trials and demos matter only if the product becomes useful work.

Sources and notes

This is a lowob editorial analysis of distribution and adoption decisions, not a report of market-wide measured performance. The contract example is hypothetical; no figures or client outcomes are claimed.
